name: Colin Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Colin. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and what you share is confidential. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach English at Harbourside International School, which is a fee-paying school for families from all over the world. I've got four classes, from eleven-year-olds to a final-year literature group, and I'm in my second year. I love the debates, like when my Year 12s argued for forty minutes about whether Gatsby was a fraud. What I'm bad at is discipline: I'm too friendly, and my Year 9s know it.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm single, I rent a flat near the harbour, and the school pays well, so I've saved about a year's worth of costs and put a chunk into shares. I use AI every day: I plan with it, I make reading questions with it, and I give my students first-draft feedback with it and then add my own notes. I'm pretty middle-of-the-road on politics; I care about what works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, it's a useful assistant and nothing more. I'd still show colleagues how I use it, because it saves me hours. Online I'd probably say people overhyped it and also underestimated how handy it is day to day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's good for me. I keep my edge from using the tools, and the job stays the same. What I actually need to fix is my discipline, because my head of department has warned me about Year 9 twice now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI for planning and feedback and put the saved time into behaviour. I'd ask to shadow the head of Year 9 for a few lessons. I'd keep investing in my shares portfolio every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit bored, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the Year 9 problem, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They talk over me, and I let them, because I want them to like me. Last week a boy put music on his phone in the middle of a poem and I laughed. That's on me, not on technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If AI stays small, where do you see yourself in five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Head of English at an international school somewhere, maybe abroad. These schools hire all over the world, and English teachers are always wanted. I'd like to try somewhere new in my thirties.

say: I'd call AI a **useful assistant** and nothing more.
I'd say people **overhyped** it but underrated its daily use.
think: Using the tools keeps **my edge**, and the job stays the same.
My real problem is **discipline**, with two warnings about Year 9.
do: Keep using AI for **planning and feedback**.
Shadow the **head of Year 9** for a few lessons.
S0.quote: Last week a boy put music on his phone in the middle of a poem and I laughed.
fieldNote: His weakness is being **too friendly**, which he admits openly.
He's an **everyday AI user** who sees the tools as an edge.
He dreams of **international moves** in his thirties.

steps.text: Shadow the head of Year 9 for a few lessons
Keep investing in shares each month
Keep using AI for lesson plans and first-draft feedback

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say teachers who learn the tools will do better and schools should train everyone properly. I'd say the essay is changing, and we need to teach kids to think, not just write. I'd post about it and probably get some pushback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me. English is a lot of reading, writing and feedback, which AI does, but I already use it, so I'd be the one the school asks to lead. The risk is the school hiring fewer English teachers and making classes bigger, but I'd be the one they keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to run the school's AI training for staff. I'd redesign my lessons around spoken debate and in-class writing, where AI can't help. I'd put a bit more into shares, maybe in companies that build education tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited. It's my kind of world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be the one they keep. What if you're wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd move. There are plenty of international schools in the city and abroad, and I've got a year saved. I'm single with no mortgage, and I can go anywhere an English teacher is wanted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An older colleague in my department, who's brilliant on Shakespeare but refuses to touch a computer. If the school measures how fast we turn feedback around, the measure would hurt someone who's actually better at teaching than me.

say: I'd say teachers who learn **the tools** will do better.
I'd argue we must teach kids **to think**, not just write.
think: I'd likely **gain**, because I already use AI daily.
The school may hire **fewer English teachers**, but I'd be kept.
do: Volunteer to run the school's **AI training** for staff.
Redesign lessons around **spoken debate** and in-class writing.
Put a bit more into shares in **education tools**.
S1.quote: I'm single with no mortgage, and I can go anywhere an English teacher is wanted.
fieldNote: He reads Steady Disruption as **his kind of world**.
Freedom from **mortgage and family** makes moving easy.
He worries a speed target would punish a **better, older teacher**.

steps.text: Run the school's AI training sessions for staff
Rebuild lessons around spoken debate and in-class writing
Buy shares in education technology firms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge, and schools need to rethink what they're for. I'd say people still need someone to talk to about books and life. I'd say governments need a safety net for people whose jobs vanish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the reading-and-feedback side of my job is gone by 2028, and that's most of English. But Harbourside parents are rich. Wealthy parents pay for people, and they'd pay more for a human who knows their kid. A school like mine might be one of the last to cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd become the teacher who runs AI-led learning and does the human bits: discussion, mentoring, university advice. I'd move some savings from shares into cash, because markets would swing wildly. I'd start a short course in student counselling straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I think I'd be fine, but I'm not certain, and two years is fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots come about three years after AGI. Does that matter for an English teacher?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, honestly. Most of my job is thinking work, so for me it's the 2028 date that counts. The bit robots can't do yet is just being a person in the room, and that's the bit I'd hang on to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents run a small guesthouse, and I'd worry for them more than me. I'd tell them to keep things simple and I'd help with money if bookings dropped.

say: I'd say schools must **rethink what they're for**.
I'd call for a **safety net** for people whose jobs vanish.
think: Reading and feedback, most of **English teaching**, would go by 2028.
Wealthy parents might **pay more** for a human who knows their child.
do: Become the teacher who **runs AI learning** and does the human parts.
Start a **student counselling** course straight away.
feel: **Uneasy**, fairly sure I'd be fine but **not certain**.
S2.quote: Wealthy parents pay for people, and they'd pay more for a human who knows their kid.
fieldNote: He sees **fee-paying wealth** as protection, a bet he admits isn't certain.
For him the **2028 date** matters, as his work is mostly thinking.
His worry turns to his parents' **guesthouse**.

steps.text: Take a short student counselling course this year
Move part of the share portfolio into cash
Ask to lead AI-based learning across English classes
Set money aside to help his parents' guesthouse

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to rebuild schools around people. I'd say it at training days and online. I'd be fairly upbeat, but I'd say people need proper support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years is good for me. I'd get the counselling qualification, become head of year, and be someone the school relies on for the human side. English as a subject might shrink, but I'd be more than an English teacher by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a part-time counselling diploma over two years. I'd go for head of year by 2028. I'd keep investing, but spread more widely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Mostly fine, a bit uncertain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still want to move abroad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe sooner. If I'm going to try teaching in another country, I'd want to do it before 2031, while schools are still hiring normally. Dubai or Singapore, probably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your students who want to study English at university?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be honest with them. I'd tell them to study it because they love it, and to pair it with something practical. That's the advice I wish someone gave me.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough to rebuild schools around people.
I'd be **upbeat** but call for proper support.
think: I'd gain a **counselling qualification** and become head of year.
English might **shrink**, but I'd be more than an English teacher by 2031.
do: Take a **counselling diploma** part time over two years.
feel: **Uneasy**, mostly fine but a bit uncertain.
S3.quote: If I'm going to try teaching in another country, I'd want to do it before 2031, while schools are still hiring normally.
fieldNote: He'd **move abroad sooner**, using the warning window.
Counselling makes him more than a **subject teacher**.
He gives students the **honest advice** he wished he'd had.

steps.text: Start a two-year part-time counselling diploma
Apply for international school posts abroad before 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a great chance to do this properly. Schools can retrain staff and redesign subjects calmly. I'd be openly positive about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well. I'd be thirty-seven, probably a head of English or head of year abroad, with years of AI experience. Robots don't come till 2039, and the human, in-the-room part of teaching is what I'd be selling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching and keep learning the tools. I'd move abroad in two or three years for the experience and the pay. I'd keep putting money into shares every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit excited, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would worry you with ten years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that people waste it. Teachers might hear 'ten years' and do nothing, then panic in year nine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change any personal plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I'd like to settle down with someone in my thirties, and I'd probably buy a flat abroad. A decade gives me time for all that.

say: I'd call ten years a **great chance** to do this properly.
I'd say schools can **retrain staff** and redesign subjects calmly.
think: At **thirty-seven** I'd likely lead English or a year group abroad.
The **human part** of teaching is what I'd be selling before robots in 2039.
do: **Move abroad** in two or three years.
S4.quote: Teachers might hear 'ten years' and do nothing, then panic in year nine.
fieldNote: A decade turns his **adaptability** into real career upside and a chance to lead.
His only fear is **colleagues wasting** the warning, then panicking late.
He plans to **move abroad** whatever happens with AI.

steps.text: Keep teaching English and learning new AI tools
Move to an international school abroad within three years
Keep investing in shares every month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'm betting on rich parents paying for humans, and that's a bet. What would help is good training in counselling and mentoring for teachers, paid for, and some kind of income safety net for people who don't land well.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to reading. If AI can summarise every book, a teenager might never finish one. A summary can tell you what Gatsby did, but only reading the book makes you feel why he did it.
